name: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital: research (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: research valued as a share of the world's childhood cancer, sickle cell and children's influenza burden.
summary: St. Jude spends about $880 million a year on research into childhood cancer and other catastrophic childhood diseases, $720 million of it from its own funds; its cancer research is about a fifth of all childhood cancer research worldwide. For its fiscal year to June 2025 this model credits each of its two branches, cancer (about 70% of the research spending) and the other diseases (sickle cell disease, influenza and basic science, about 30%), with St. Jude's share of what a year of the field's research does to the world's burden of those diseases (the deaths in it valued by age at the site's value of a death, the illness as healthy years), anchored on published returns to medical research. The result, about 0.005 years of healthy life per $1,000, is far below the site's global-health median (about a thousandth of it) because research pays off only after a long lag, through uptake by others, and the field's progress is shared among all its funders. Both branches are discounted for missing data, since St. Jude's research has no outcome measure of its own; the result is mostly uncertainty, dominated by judgment (the chance a year's research yields an advance and the share of the burden it averts), and its plausible range spans about two-hundredfold (0.0004 to 0.07).

source.title: charityevals' estimate: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, research (FY2025)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ programme expenses, both net of insurers' and grant money)
rows.explainer: Spreads fundraising and administration over the programmes St. Jude pays for itself: donations pay for all the fundraising, so the overhead goes on the own-funded spending only (1.74; 1.61 over all programme spending). It splits the own-funded research into the two branches.

rows.label: Cancer branch: childhood and adolescent cancer, DALYs a year worldwide (ages 0-19, GBD 2023)

source.title: Force et al. (GBD 2023 Childhood Cancer Collaborators), Global burden of cancer in children and adolescents aged 0-19 years, 1990-2023, The Lancet 2026
source.quote: 144 000 deaths (131 000-162 000), and 11·7 million (10·7-13·2) DALYs due to childhood cancer

rows.explainer: The burden St. Jude's cancer research addresses, worldwide, since its protocols and drugs travel; GBD 2023, the latest round (GBD 2017 gave 11.5 million, 82.2% of it in low, low-middle and middle Socio-demographic Index countries, where access, not knowledge, limits survival: ca_share_burden_addressable takes that into account). Nearly all of it is years of life lost to 144,000 deaths a year, valued below by age at the site's value of a death (ca_deaths_per_daly); the rest is illness (ca_yld_share). The study's 95% uncertainty interval is the range.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: sickle cell disease, DALYs a year worldwide (for reading and weighting)
rows.explainer: Context, for the reading averages only (not on the result's path). Judgment built from two GBD 2021 analyses, since the papers give no global DALY total. Thomson et al. (GBD 2021 Sickle Cell Disease Collaborators, Lancet Haematology 2023, https://doi.org/10.1016/s2352-3026(23)00118-7): 515,000 babies born with sickle cell disease a year and 376,000 deaths a year (303,000-467,000) once deaths sickle cell disease causes through infections and other conditions are counted, 34,400 assigned to it as the single underlying cause; 81,100 of them under five. Sahu et al. (Blood 2025, GBD 2021 DALYs, https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2025-2601): Nigeria alone 'an estimated 2.1 million SCD-attributable DALYs' with about 100,000 of the births, a fifth of the world's, so about 11 million DALYs worldwide if the rest of the world carries it alike. 5 million if only part of the total-mortality burden counts (the cause-specific deaths alone would give about 2.5 million), 25 million at the high end of the total-mortality estimate with India's and the Americas' longer-lived patients. Read only to weight the branch's reading averages and its two diseases' shares: the outcome is built from the deaths (nc_scd_deaths_per_year, valued by age) and the illness (nc_scd_yld_per_year), since 376,000 deaths at their ages would by themselves carry more than 11 million years of life lost.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: deaths from sickle cell disease a year worldwide (total mortality)

source.title: Thomson et al. (GBD 2021 Sickle Cell Disease Collaborators), Global, regional, and national prevalence and mortality burden of sickle cell disease, 2000-2021, Lancet Haematology 2023
source.quote: total sickle cell disease mortality burden was nearly 11-times higher at 376 000 (303 000-467 000)

rows.explainer: Deaths sickle cell disease causes, directly or through infections and other conditions it makes deadly; 34,400 are assigned to it as the single underlying cause. Valued by age (nc_scd_value_per_death).

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: years lived with disability from sickle cell disease a year worldwide
rows.explainer: Judgment: 7.74 million people live with sickle cell disease (Thomson et al. 2023) at an average disability weight of about 0.08 across chronic anaemia (GBD 2019 weights: moderate 0.052, severe 0.149), pain crises and stroke, about 0.6 million years a year; 0.3-1.2 million.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: influenza lower respiratory infections in children under five, DALYs a year worldwide
rows.explainer: St. Jude's influenza work (a WHO collaborating centre for the ecology of animal influenza, surveillance, vaccine and antiviral research) bears on influenza at every age; this branch counts the under-fives, the paediatric burden the hospital's mission names, so it is low if the work also cuts adult influenza deaths (about 85% of the GBD influenza death toll). 2021 was a low influenza year after the pandemic; the GBD interval is the range.

source.title: Zhang et al., Global burden of influenza lower respiratory tract infections in children younger than 5 years from 1990 to 2021, Journal of Thoracic Disease 2026 (GBD 2021)
source.quote: influenza LRTIs caused 27,615 [95% uncertainty interval (UI): 20,128-36,852] deaths and 2,460,833 (95% UI: 1,796,287-3,280,725) DALYs in children under five in 2021

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: deaths from influenza lower respiratory infections under five a year
rows.explainer: 27,615 (GBD 2021), from the DALYs and the shared deaths-per-DALY figure.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: years lived with disability from children's influenza a year
Non-cancer branch: burden of the diseases the targeted research addresses, DALYs a year
rows.explainer: Sickle cell disease and children's influenza. HIV, neurological and immune disorders, which St. Jude also studies, have no burden counted here; their research enters through nc_other_research_ratio below.

rows.label: Burden addressed, both branches (for reading)
rows.explainer: The two branches' burdens together, for reading; each branch uses its own.

rows.label: Cancer branch: share of the world's childhood cancer burden one successful year's advance averts once adopted
rows.explainer: Judgment. A typical advance of the kind St. Jude produces (a risk-adapted leukaemia protocol, a targeted drug for one subtype, a better brain-tumour regimen) raises survival by several points for one cancer: in the high-income countries that adopt it at once (only about 6% of the world's childhood cancer burden in GBD 2023) that is a few per cent of their burden; in upper-middle-income countries (China, much of Latin America, a large part of the burden) referral centres adopt such protocols within years, and in poorer countries it spreads more slowly with the protocols partners adapt. 2% of the world's burden; 0.8% for an advance in a rare cancer, 6% for one in leukaemia or brain tumours that middle-income units take up. Partner units' adoption of new advances is credited here; St. Jude Global's survival gain (the patient care model) counts better delivery of existing care, so it isn't credited twice.

rows.label: Cancer branch: chance a year of the field's research yields such an advance
rows.explainer: Judgment, calibrated jointly with ca_share_burden_addressable and ca_years_brought_forward so that the field's result per dollar (field_dalys_per_dollar) matches the research-returns reference class; the split between the three is a judgment. US childhood cancer mortality fell by more than half from 1975 to 2022, about 1.8% a year (National Cancer Institute, https://www.cancer.gov/types/childhood-cancers/child-adolescent-cancers-fact-sheet), most of it from treatment advances, and the world's falls more slowly; UK cancer research earned a health-gain return of about 10% a year with a lag of about 15 years (Glover et al., BMC Medicine 2014, https://doi.org/10.1186/1741-7015-12-99). ca_share_burden_addressable × ca_p_success is 0.5% of the world's burden a year at the best guesses. A quarter of years bring such an advance; low if most of the year's work is basic science that never reaches practice, high if the year's clinical trials change protocols.

rows.label: Cancer branch: years the advance comes earlier because of this year's research
rows.explainer: Judgment: how much later the advance would come if this year's research weren't done, with others' work going on (Convention 5: the counterfactual question is answered here, so ca_counterfactual_adj is 1). No published study estimates years brought forward (the returns-to-research studies estimate lags and rates of return), so it is calibrated jointly with ca_p_success and ca_share_burden_addressable through the check rows (ca_burden_fall_per_year, field_dalys_per_dollar); the split between the three is a judgment. 5, above the medical-research template's default of 3 (1-10), because childhood cancer is a small field in which St. Jude is about a fifth of the funding and advances come through long trial series (St. Jude's Total Therapy XV ran 2000-07, XVI 2007-17), so a year's work is a larger part of the next generation of protocols than in a broad field; 2 for crowded fields (leukaemia), 10 for rare tumours St. Jude almost alone studies.

rows.label: Cancer branch: years from the research to the advance being in practice
rows.explainer: Judgment on the reference class: about 17 years from research to practice (Morris, Wooding and Grant, J R Soc Med 2011), about 15 for UK cancer research (Glover et al. 2014); St. Jude's spending includes many clinical trials, whose results change protocols within a few years, beside basic science with the long lag. 12 (6-17).

rows.label: Cancer branch: the wait, discounted
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Cancer branch: years brought forward, discounted
rows.explainer: Each year brought forward and the wait before it, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Cancer branch: DALYs averted by a year of the field's research
rows.explainer: Before St. Jude's share and the adjustments.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: share of the burden one successful year's advance averts once adopted
rows.explainer: Judgment, on the same reference class as the cancer branch (ca_share_burden_addressable, 2%), lower because the burden sits where access, not knowledge, limits care: sickle cell deaths are mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, where newborn screening, penicillin and hydroxyurea, all decades old, reach few children (Piel et al., Lancet Haematology Commission 2023, https://doi.org/10.1016/s2352-3026(23)00096-0), and the curative gene therapies St. Jude helped develop cost millions per patient; influenza advances (vaccine strain selection, antivirals) spread through existing programmes. 1.5% of the burden; 0.4% for an advance only rich countries can use, 5% for one in cheap supportive care or vaccines that middle-income countries take up.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: chance a year of the field's research yields such an advance
rows.explainer: Judgment on the reference class of the cancer branch (ca_p_success, 25%) and the published returns to medical research (UK cardiovascular and mental-health research earned health-gain returns of about 9% and 7% a year, Health Economics Research Group, Office of Health Economics and RAND Europe, Medical Research: What's it worth?, 2008). Sickle cell care moved slowly for decades before hydroxyurea and gene therapy, so lower than cancer's: 20%, 5% if most of the year's work is basic science, 50% if its trials change practice.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: years the advance comes earlier because of this year's research
rows.explainer: Judgment, the medical-research template's default (3, 1-10), since no published study estimates years brought forward: influenza research is a crowded field (1-2 years), sickle cell disease a neglected one where St. Jude is among few large funders (up to 10). It answers the counterfactual question (Convention 5), so nc_counterfactual_adj is 1.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: years from the research to the advance being in practice
rows.explainer: Judgment on the translation lag of about 17 years (Morris, Wooding and Grant, J R Soc Med 2011, https://doi.org/10.1258/jrsm.2011.110180), shorter for clinical trials of existing drugs (hydroxyurea dosing in children) than for gene therapy or new vaccines: 12 (6-20), as the cancer branch.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: the wait, discounted
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: years brought forward, discounted
rows.explainer: Each year brought forward and the wait before it, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: DALYs averted by a year of the field's research on these diseases
rows.explainer: Before St. Jude's share and the adjustments.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: share of the diseases' deaths and illness a year of the field's research averts, over the years brought forward
rows.explainer: The chain's fraction, applied to the deaths and to the illness separately.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: share of the non-cancer research on sickle cell disease and influenza
rows.explainer: Judgment from St. Jude's departments outside oncology: haematology (sickle cell disease, gene therapy, bone-marrow failure) and infectious diseases (influenza, the WHO collaborating centre) are the two largest; the rest is neurobiology, developmental neurobiology, structural biology, immunology and HIV. Half (30-70%).

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: what a dollar of the rest of the non-cancer research does, relative to the targeted research
rows.explainer: Judgment. The rest (neurobiology, structural and developmental biology, immunology, HIV) is mostly basic science with no single burden to count: its results reach patients through the cancer, blood-disorder and infection work, and some (structural biology of viral proteins, immunology) are part of them. Half the targeted research's value per dollar; a tenth if little of it reaches practice, as much if it does as well.

rows.label: Non-cancer branch: the rest of the non-cancer research, as a multiple of the targeted research's DALYs
rows.explainer: The targeted research counts once; the rest of the branch's spending counts at nc_other_research_ratio of its value per dollar.

rows.label: Share of the burden one successful year's advance averts, burden-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Weighted by each branch's burden; each branch uses its own.

rows.label: Chance a year's research yields an advance, weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (ca_disease_dalys_per_year * ca_share_burden_addressable * ca_p_success + nc_disease_dalys_per_year * nc_share_burden_addressable * nc_p_success) / (disease_dalys_per_year * share_burden_addressable)
rows.explainer: Weighted by each branch's burden addressable; each branch uses its own.

rows.label: Years brought forward, outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Each branch uses its own.

rows.label: Years until the advance is in practice, outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Each branch uses its own.

rows.label: The wait, discounted (reading row at the average wait)
rows.explainer: The average wait discounted at the shared rate, for reading; each branch discounts its own (ca_wait_discount, nc_wait_discount).

rows.label: Years brought forward, discounted (reading row at the averages)
rows.explainer: For reading; each branch discounts its own (ca_discounted_years, nc_discounted_years).

rows.label: DALYs averted by a year of the fields' research, both branches (for reading)
rows.explainer: Each branch's DALYs before St. Jude's share and the adjustments, at GBD's DALYs (for reading; the non-cancer outcome is built from its deaths and illness).

rows.label: Advocacy: people per year the policy won or pressed would affect
rows.explainer: 0: St. Jude runs no policy or advocacy campaigns; its public messaging is ALSAC's fundraising (counted as overhead).

rows.label: Advocacy: DALYs averted per person affected per year
rows.explainer: 0: no advocacy branch (adv_people_affected_per_year).

rows.label: Advocacy: probability the policy changes because of this work
rows.explainer: 0: no advocacy branch.

rows.label: Advocacy: years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: 0: no advocacy branch.

rows.label: Advocacy: discounted years of impact
Expected DALYs averted by advocacy (before adjustments)
Cancer branch: trust in the effect (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Judgment, the family's default (0.7), on the validity of the chain's reference class: the UK's return is one country's record over one period, with its own attribution assumptions (17% of gains to UK research), transferred to childhood cancer worldwide. St. Jude's record (Total Therapy trials took leukaemia survival from under 10% to over 90%) is why the discount isn't larger. The absence of an outcome measure of St. Jude's own is the missing-data discount, not this.

rows.label: Cancer branch: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: what would have happened without this year's research is in ca_years_brought_forward (Convention 5), so it isn't discounted again.

rows.label: Cancer branch: all funders' spending on childhood cancer research a year, worldwide
rows.explainer: Judgment built up from its parts: the US National Cancer Institute 'spent more than $600 million on childhood cancer' in FY2023 (St. Baldrick's, https://blog.stbaldricks.org/?p=36179), St. Jude's own cancer research about $500 million, other US children's hospitals' and charities' own funds (St. Baldrick's, Alex's Lemonade Stand, Dana-Farber, CHOP and others) a few hundred million, Europe and the rest of the world (national research councils, Children with Cancer UK, the Princess Máxima Centre, EU programmes) about $500 million, and drug companies' paediatric trials (required by US and EU paediatric rules) several hundred million.

rows.label: Cancer branch: St. Jude's share of the field's funding
rows.explainer: St. Jude's own cancer research ÷ all funders' childhood cancer research (Convention 2): about a fifth. The NIH grants St. Jude receives are counted in the field, not in St. Jude's share.

rows.label: Cancer branch: discount for an outcome not measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): the effect of a year's research is a judgment on the research-returns literature, not St. Jude's own record traced to practice.

rows.label: Cash and investments at 30 June 2025

source.title: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and ALSAC, combined financial statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, Deloitte & Touche LLP)
source.page: p. 3, combined statements of financial position (in 000s)
source.quote: CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS $ 557,709 ... UNRESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 8,444,862 ... RESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 1,587,521

rows.explainer: Cash ($557.7 million), unrestricted investments ($8,444.9 million) and investments restricted by donors ($1,587.5 million): about three and three-quarter years of spending held in reserve.

rows.label: Years a donation waits before St. Jude spends it
rows.explainer: The reserves ÷ a year's spending, as the template asks for a charity that spends from reserves: 3.7 years. St. Jude holds its reserves by policy and spends from donations, bequests and investment returns, so a dollar given today adds to the pool and is, on average, spent about this much later. While it waits it is invested (interest_yield), which almost cancels the discount.

rows.label: Long-run nominal return on the invested reserves
rows.explainer: Judgment. The reserves earned $939.3 million in FY2025 on about $9.6 billion of investments (p. 4; average of the two year-ends, p. 3), 9.7%, and $856.7 million in FY2024: two strong market years. Long-run returns of diversified endowment portfolios have averaged about 6-7% a year nominal over ten-year periods (US college and university endowment studies, NACUBO-Commonfund); 6.5%, 4% in a weak decade, 9% at the recent returns.

rows.label: Yearly rise in the cost of care and research

rows.label: The whole field's research: healthy years per dollar, before St. Jude's share and the donor steps (for reading)
rows.explainer: A check against the reference class: what a dollar of all funders' childhood cancer research does in this chain, discounted. Glover et al. (BMC Medicine 2014, https://doi.org/10.1186/1741-7015-12-99) put UK public and charity cancer research at £15 billion over 1970-2009 (2011/12 prices) and the QALYs gained from cancer care 1991-2010 at 5.9 million, 17% of their net value attributable to UK research, with a lag of about 15 years: about 1 million QALYs from the research of roughly 1976-1995, about a third of the £15 billion if spending grew steadily (about £5 billion, our reading, not the paper's figure), some 2e-4 QALYs per 2011/12 pound, about 1e-4 per 2024 dollar undiscounted, about 5-6e-5 once the 15-year wait is discounted at the shared rate; this row is about 5e-5. The two measure different things, so the match is a sanity bound, not a validation: Glover counts the UK's health gains only and credits research (17% of them) with the gains as they happened, while this chain counts the world's burden and credits a year's research only with the years it brings an advance forward; it is in DALYs before the deaths are valued by age.

rows.label: Check: share of the world's childhood cancer burden a year of the field's research removes once in practice
rows.explainer: A check against the observed trend, which fits the chain better than the returns studies: US childhood cancer mortality fell by more than half from 1975 to 2022, about 1.8% a year (National Cancer Institute), most of it from treatment advances, but high-income countries carry only about 6% of the world's childhood cancer burden (GBD 2023), so that alone is about 0.1% of the world's burden a year. Worldwide, childhood cancer deaths fell 27% from 1990 to 2023 (Force et al., Lancet 2026), about 1% a year with population growth, from advances and from better access together. If about half of that is the field's new knowledge, a year's advances remove roughly 0.3-0.7% of the burden; this row is 0.5%.
